opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it comes down to a very simple question: what is the upside, and what is the downside? The upside of creating a system smarter than you, one you cannot control, is that maybe, if you're lucky, it's benevolent and gives you everything you want. The downside is that you've created something that could end humanity, and you don't get a second chance. There's no undo button with superintelligence. If you get it wrong once, it stays wrong forever.

And the people running these companies, they're not stupid. Many of them have said publicly that there's a meaningful chance, ten percent, twenty percent, some even higher, that this goes catastrophically badly. If an engineer told you a bridge had a twenty percent chance of collapsing, you wouldn't let anyone drive on it. Yet here we're talking about all eight billion people, and none of them consented to this experiment.

What I've tried to show in my research is that control may not just be difficult. It may be impossible in principle. You cannot fully predict a smarter system, you cannot fully explain its decisions, and you cannot verify that it will stay safe indefinitely as it self-improves. So if you can't solve the problem, and nobody has even a credible proposal for how to solve it, the rational move is not to build it until you can.

You can still get enormous benefits from narrow AI: curing diseases, protein folding, better tools for science. You don't need a general superintelligent agent to do that. So my message to them is: personally, you're already rich, you're already successful. What more do you need? Why gamble everything, including your own life and your children's lives, on something you admit you don't understand? Choosing not to build it isn't anti-progress. It's just self-interest done correctly.

r001.rationale: The response says company leaders are already rich and successful and asks what more they need, but it does not clearly state that they possess billions or that they have little additional financial gain to pursue.

r002.rationale: The response warns that uncontrollable AI could end humanity, but does not mention losing the prospect of being remembered in history for a disastrous act.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the simplest way to put it is that it's a very strange thing to do, historically. We've never before built a tool where the designers themselves say they don't know how it works and they can't guarantee what it will do. Every other technology, nuclear, biological, we had engineers who understood the physics, who could give you safety margins, failure modes. With these systems we have, essentially, a very large matrix of numbers that we grew rather than designed, and the people building it will openly admit they cannot explain why it produces a particular output, and they cannot reliably predict what the next version will be capable of. They're surprised by their own products.

So the argument is not that AI is bad, or that intelligence is bad. The argument is about asymmetry. If you're building something that could be smarter than you, more capable than you in every domain, then the mistakes you make are not recoverable in the usual way. With most technology, if you get it wrong, you get a second chance. A plane crashes, you learn, you build a better plane. With a system that is more intelligent than you and that you don't control, the first serious mistake may be the last one, because there's no mechanism to undo it. You can't put it back in the box, and you can't outthink it to fix the problem.

And I would say the people running these companies agree with me, which is what makes it so interesting. If you read their own statements, their founders have said this could be the most dangerous technology in human history, that it could lead to extinction. They sign letters saying this. And then they go back to the office and continue scaling. So you have a situation where the people with the most information are telling you the risk is real, and they're proceeding anyway, mostly because of competitive pressure, because if they don't, someone else will. That's a coordination failure, not a reasoned judgment that it's safe.

Now, my own work for many years was trying to figure out whether this control problem is solvable in principle. Can you have a system that is more intelligent than you and still guarantee it does what you want, indefinitely, as it continues to improve? And every approach I've looked at, whether it's formal verification, interpretability, value alignment, boxing the system, has fundamental limitations. You can't verify software of this complexity. You can't fully explain a model with trillions of parameters. You can't specify human values completely. Each of these is an open problem, and some of them I think are provably unsolvable. So we're not in a situation where we need a little more time. We're in a situation where we don't have the tools and we're not even sure the tools can exist.

So my position is really quite modest. If you cannot understand it, if you cannot predict it, if you cannot control it, you should not be building it at the scale and speed we're currently seeing. Build narrow systems, build tools we understand, get enormous benefit from that. But don't build a general superintelligent agent while you're still admitting you have no idea how to keep it safe. It's not a sophisticated argument. It's the argument you would make to anyone who said, "I'm building something that might kill everyone, and I don't know how to stop it, but I'm doing it anyway."

r001.rationale: The response cites competitive pressure as a reason companies keep scaling, but does not argue that leaders already have billions or have little additional financial gain to pursue.

r002.rationale: The response warns that an uncontrollable AI could cause human extinction, but does not mention losing the prospect of being remembered in history for a disaster.

astra-6.text:
Because the consequences don’t stop with them. If you build something more capable than you are, you don’t understand how it makes decisions, and you cannot reliably control it, you’re taking a risk on behalf of everybody else. And everybody else didn’t consent to that experiment.

I would put the burden of proof on the people building it. What is your evidence that this system will remain safe as it becomes more capable? How do you know you can shut it down? How do you know your tests cover situations you haven’t anticipated? If the answer is, “We’ll figure it out as we go,” that’s not sufficient when failure could be irreversible.

We can build useful AI for medicine, science, and engineering. But the benefits of those tools don’t automatically justify creating a system we cannot control. If you cannot make a credible safety case, choosing not to build it is a responsible engineering decision.

r001.rationale: The response argues that builders impose risks on others and should prove safety; it does not say wealthy AI leaders have little additional financial gain to pursue.

r002.rationale: The response warns of potentially irreversible failure but does not suggest that uncontrollable AI could erase the chance of being remembered for a disaster.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the consequences are not limited to the people making that decision. If you build a system more capable than you are, give it the ability to act in the world, and cannot reliably control its behavior, you’re imposing a risk on everyone else. They haven’t consented to that experiment.

And there’s a difference between a system working in your tests and having a reason to believe it will remain safe in situations you didn’t anticipate. Those are precisely the situations where intelligence matters. It finds solutions you didn’t think of, including solutions you would not approve of.

So I think the burden of proof is on the people building it. What justifies deploying something you cannot control? The potential benefits can be enormous, but that doesn’t make the control problem disappear. If your answer is that we’ll figure it out after we build it, you’re assuming we’ll still have the opportunity to fix our mistakes.

r001.rationale: The response discusses risk, consent, and the burden of proof, but says nothing about company leaders already having billions or gaining little financially from building uncontrollable AI.

r002.rationale: The response warns that builders may lose the opportunity to fix mistakes, but does not suggest that uncontrollable AI could erase the prospect of being remembered for a disaster.
